extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim additional elements integrate a recited judicial exception into a practical application (Alice/Mayo Step 2A Prong Two) for U.S. patent eligibility. Describes relevant considerations, examples, anti-patterns, and the evaluative procedure examiners should follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim as a whole integrates the judicial exception into a practical application when it applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim integrates the exception into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If it does not integrate the exception, the claim is directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis under Step 2B. Evaluate integration using the considerations listed in the MPEP (subsection I).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination of elements) may integrate the exception into a practical application when the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or improves another technology or technical field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the specification to see if disclosure provides sufficient detail so one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement. The specification need not explicitly say 'improvement' but must make it apparent; conclusory assertions are insufficient. The claim must reflect the components/steps that provide the improvement (need not recite the improvement in explicit words). This consideration is evaluated without regard to whether elements are conventional in Step 2A Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using a judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that apply or use the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition can integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, etc. Vanda illustrates using a natural-law relationship (genotype-drug risk) to safely treat patients (dose adjustment) rather than merely gathering data, supporting eligibility at Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing the exception with or using it in conjunction with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a particular machine or manufacture as an integral part of the claim can indicate integration of the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed machine/manufacture is integral to the invention and how it interacts with the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(b)). Mere recitation of a machine without meaningful integration is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that effect a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can indicate the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed steps materially change an article's state/thing as part of the claimed invention (see MPEP § 2106.05(c)). The transformation must be meaningful relative to the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying or using the exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linking to a technological environment
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element may integrate the exception into a practical application if it applies or uses the judicial exception in some meaningful way beyond generally linking its use to a particular technological environment or field of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for meaningful limits that go beyond 'apply it' or mere environment/field recitations. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for examples and further explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merely reciting application instructions or using a computer as a tool (does not integrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recitations are treated as insufficient post-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)). Examiners should identify whether claimed steps are mere invocation of a computer or instructions to apply an exception without meaningful technical integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (does not integrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., routine data gathering or post-solution steps that do not materially apply the exception) does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to Parker v. Flook where lack of specifics for implementation supported finding additional elements insignificant. See MPEP § 2106.05(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generally linking the exception to a technological environment or field of use (does not integrate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, without more, does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A field-of-use limitation or mere technological environment linking is insufficient (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)). The additional elements must meaningfully limit the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of conventionality analysis in Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong Two specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should give weight to all additional elements when evaluating integration, whether or not they are conventional. Well-understood, routine, conventional activity may nonetheless integrate the exception into a practical application under Prong Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality/tangibility is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2A Prong Two; tangible implementation alone does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Alice: presence of a computer or physical element is 'beside the point.' Conversely, non-physical elements do not necessarily doom eligibility (see Enfish, McRO examples). Evaluate functional integration rather than mere tangibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations as a relevant factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Specificity of the claim limitations is relevant to evaluating considerations such as use of a particular machine, particular transformation, and whether the limitations are mere instructions to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity is not a standalone consideration, but detailed claim limitations (or lack thereof) can inform whether the additional elements meaningfully integrate the exception. Parker v. Flook illustrates that failure to explain specifics can support a finding of insignificant post-solution activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prong Two evaluation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate integration into a practical application by: (1) identifying any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s); and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they integrate the exception into a practical application using one or more of the listed considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a weighing test—type or number of considerations applied is not decisive. Evaluate significance of additional elements relative to the invention and how limitations interact. If claim as a whole integrates the exception, the additional limitations impose a meaningful limit and claim is eligible at Step 2A. Examiners must analyze each claim separately; dependent claims may differ in eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate each claim on its own facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately based on the particular elements recited; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One claim may be ineligible while another dependent claim with additional elements may be eligible because it integrates the exception into a practical application or amounts to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and case-law guidance (use to inform considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case examples illustrate application of Prong Two considerations — e.g., Solutran (claims directed to abstract idea), Finjan (virus scanning improved computer functionality), Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory, SRI (improvements to computer/technology), Vanda (treatment/prophylaxis using genotype info).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these cases to analogize whether claimed additional elements show improvement, meaningful application, or are merely conventional/insignificant. Review MPEP §§ 2106.05(a)-(h) for additional case discussions and application of considerations.
